I spent two weeks chasing a single ghost checkout bug on STRAYED.

We were setting up our custom payment flow and the checkout was lagging. Users would hit pay, get their money deducted, but the order confirmation screen would just hang. Tbh, it was incredibly frustrating because on paper, everything looked perfectly clean.

The issue turned out to be how we handled Razorpay webhooks. The webhook was triggering a confirmation email before the local database write fully completed. This caused a weird race condition that kept mobile users staring at a spinning loader.

To fix it, we refactored our state machine to prioritize optimistic UI updates. Now, the client assumes success immediately after the gateway callback, while a silent database query handles any delays in the background. Latency dropped to almost zero.

It made me realize how much of good UX is just hiding backend latency from the user.

How do you handle webhook race conditions without breaking your client-side state?

#webdev #javascript #razerpay

Waiting for a backend response to update a cart UI feels incredibly outdated.

When you add an item to your cart on Amazon, the UI updates instantly. There is no spinner, no lag, and no waiting for a server confirmation.

I wanted that exact same zero-latency feel for STRAYED.

To get there, I implemented optimistic client-side updates in our frontend. When a user clicks 'Add to Cart', we immediately update the local React State to reflect the new item, while the actual API request to our MedusaJS backend runs silently in the background.

If the server request fails for some rare reason, we gracefully roll back the UI state and show a quick notification. But 99% of the time, the user experiences an instant, snappy transition.

It is a small detail, but these micro-interactions are what separate clean, premium products from clunky web pages.

MedusaJS subscribers make event-driven architecture incredibly easy to implement.

When a customer places an order, we need to trigger several actions at once. We have to update our inventory in Odoo, send a confirmation email, and log the transaction for our accounting records.

Instead of packing all this logic into a single bloated controller, I used MedusaJS subscribers. I created an order subscriber that listens for the order placed event and runs these tasks asynchronously.

This keeps our main checkout API response super fast because the server does not wait for third-party APIs to respond before confirming the order. If one of the background tasks fails, it does not crash the user's checkout flow.

Using event-driven patterns on the backend has completely changed how I think about system design. ⚡

pending.post_text: I spent three days debugging a recursive inventory sync between our Postgres database and Odoo. It turned out to be a simple timezone offset issue. Our server was running in UTC, but the Odoo ERP import utility was expecting IST for our product release timestamps. Every time we pushed an update for Prettiva, the inventory count would drift by exactly five and a half hours. It meant products were appearing as out of stock while they were actually sitting live in the warehouse. Seeing a bunch of zeros in the dashboard when you know the shelves are full is a special kind of panic. I fixed it by standardizing every timestamp across the entire pipeline to ISO 8601 strings before they ever hit the database layer. Now the sync happens at 2 AM every day without any drift. Debugging time synchronization is tedious, but it is the kind of silent work that keeps a business running while you sleep. I spent four hours last Tuesday debugging a circular dependency in our database migrations. 

We were trying to expand the STRAYED inventory schema to handle localized pricing, but the new table relationships conflicted with our legacy audit logs. Every time I ran the migration script, it would hang midway and revert changes. 

I realized the issue was not the code logic, but the order in which the ORM was attempting to execute the primary key constraints. It was trying to reference a table that hadn't been fully indexed yet. 

I manually split the migration into two separate phases and added a forced pause between the schema modification and the data migration. It was a tedious fix, but the system became much more stable afterward. 

Database integrity is one of those things that seems boring until you lose an entire afternoon trying to undo a broken migration.
